q: A server has thirty seconds to judge how heavy an unfamiliar wine will feel in the mouth. Which figure on the label is the most useful clue?
opts: The number of varieties in the blend
exp: Alcohol adds viscosity and warmth of its own, and it also stands in for ripeness, so a wine at fourteen and a half will almost always feel fuller than one at eleven. Sugar and oak add weight too, which makes it a guide rather than a rule, but it is the fastest guide a label offers.

q: Echoing a quality the dish already carries and supplying one it lacks are the two oldest strategies in pairing. A very sweet wine is set beside a salty blue cheese: which strategy is that, and why?
opts: It supplies what the plate lacks, since the wine is the drier of the two
It supplies what the plate lacks, since nothing in the cheese is sweet
It echoes the plate, since the cheese is as sweet as the wine
It echoes the plate, since the wine is as salty as the cheese
exp: Echoing means the same quality turns up on both sides of the table, so the glass repeats something the cook has already put on the plate. The other strategy works the opposite way round, with the wine bringing a quality the dish has none of at all, which is why sugar registers so loudly against salt. Naming which of the two a pairing rests on is the quickest way to explain it to a guest.

q: A basket of whitebait comes out of the fryer, hot and glistening with oil. Which pour keeps the palate fresh to the last one?
opts: A soft, heavily oaked white with very little acidity
exp: Anything straight out of the fryer wants the glass cold, dry and lively. The heavy red piles weight on weight, the sweet wine turns the whole plate cloying, and the soft oaked white brings nothing to reset the palate with, so the same answer covers tempura, fried chicken and fish and chips.

q: Duck rillettes and a coarse pork terrine are set out with cornichons and mustard. Which red is the easier partner?
opts: A sweet red made from grapes dried on straw mats
A light, high-acid red served slightly cool
An old and delicate red at the peak of its life
A heavily oaked red at fifteen percent
exp: Fat and salt want freshness set against them rather than more weight, and a light chill sharpens a simple red further. The old bottle is the real trap on a list like this: a coarse terrine with mustard beside it tramples a wine whose whole appeal is subtlety.

q: A smooth chicken liver parfait is spread thickly on toast, unctuous and faintly metallic. Which glass is the traditional foil?
opts: A neutral dry white with low acidity
exp: Sweetness meets the richness instead of fighting it, while the acid underneath stops the pairing turning heavy after two mouthfuls. Tannin against liver tends to read metallic, and the neutral white simply disappears under the fat.

q: Fried chicken is ordered at the bar and the guest wants red rather than white. Which suggestion does the least damage?
opts: A heavily oaked red at fifteen percent
A young red with firm, drying tannin
A juicy, low-tannin red served cool
exp: A stated preference is worth working with rather than around, and a red can be made to fit here by choosing one that behaves like a white: cool, fruity and light on grip. Tannin and oak are what turn fried food harsh in the mouth, so the recommendation is really about avoiding those two.

q: Hot-smoked salmon, oily and heavy with smoke, opens the meal. Which white is the safer choice?
opts: An unoaked white with firm acidity
A warm, high-alcohol white at fifteen percent
exp: Two lots of smoke do not cancel each other, they accumulate, so a barrel-heavy wine beside smoked fish tastes acrid within a couple of mouthfuls. Keeping the wine clean and sharp leaves the smoke where the cook put it, and gives the oil in the fish something to be cut by.

q: Ribs come out of the smoker lacquered in a sweet, sticky sauce. Which red suits them?
opts: A lean, austere red with searing acidity
A pale, delicate red at twelve percent
A ripe, fruit-forward red with soft tannin
A tannic red from a cool climate, aged in new oak
exp: A sauce with sugar in it needs a wine whose fruit reads sweet, or the wine turns hard and sour beside it. Lean and austere is exactly the wrong direction here, and firm tannin against smoke and char comes across as bitter rather than as structure.

q: Of the snacks a bar can put in front of a guest holding a glass of wine, which is the most obliging?
exp: Salt is the friendliest thing you can set beside a glass: it makes fruit read more clearly and takes the edge off whatever bitterness the wine carries. The other three each fight the glass in their own way, which is why a bowl of nuts or olives is the standing default in every wine bar in the world.

q: Green olives and a glass of red are ordered together and the wine turns unpleasantly metallic. What is the usual fix?
opts: Serve the same red much warmer
Add a little ice to the red
Decant the red for an hour to soften it
exp: Brine and tannin are a poor combination, and no amount of handling the same bottle repairs it, because the problem is the match rather than the condition of the wine. Olives sit far more happily with something dry, sharp and unoaked, which is why they belong beside a fino or a manzanilla as naturally as they do beside a cold glass of white.

q: The kitchen sends out a slice of tarte Tatin, caramelised and very sweet. Which of these bottles will taste sour beside it?
exp: Sweetness is judged against whatever came immediately before it, so a dry wine tasted after a caramelised pudding loses its fruit and shows only acid and alcohol. The other three all carry enough sugar of their own to hold their ground, which is the whole reason dessert wines exist.

q: Sweet-and-sour pork, glazed teriyaki chicken and a mango salad all set the wine list the same problem. What is it?
opts: An unusually high level of salt
exp: Sweetness on a savoury plate is easy to miss when reading a menu, and it changes the recommendation completely, because a dry wine beside it loses its fruit exactly as it would beside a pudding. A wine with a trace of sugar of its own, or a red with very ripe fruit, keeps its shape.

q: Ice cream is on the dessert list and the sommelier hesitates before pouring anything with it. What is the difficulty?
opts: It contains no sugar to speak of
The cold numbs the palate to the wine
Its acidity outruns any sweet wine
exp: A very cold spoonful shuts the palate down for a moment, so whatever follows registers faintly and an expensive glass is wasted. Pouring alongside rather than after, and choosing something intensely flavoured, are the two usual ways around it.

q: Strawberries and cream close a long summer lunch. Which pour is the safest?
opts: A sweet, nutty fortified white at eighteen percent
exp: Fruit at the end of a meal reads sweet, so the glass has to bring at least as much sugar or it turns tart in the mouth. Sugar on its own is not the whole answer, though, because the wine also has to stay light and fresh: a warming, nutty style buries fruit this delicate whatever its sweetness. Demi-sec sparkling wine and Moscato d'Asti both do the job at very different prices.

q: A young, firmly tannic red is showing hard and drying on its own before dinner. Which plate would flatter it most?
exp: Protein and fat take the edge off astringency, which is why a red that seems punishing on its own settles down beside red meat. The other three give the tannin nothing to work against, so it stays exactly as hard as it was and the wine gets the blame.

q: A vegetarian guest asks for a red as substantial as the one their neighbour is drinking with steak. Which dish on the menu would carry it?
opts: A green salad dressed sharply with lemon and shallot
A rich bean and lentil stew
exp: Weight, texture and a little fat are what a big red needs, and none of the three requires meat to supply them; pulses cooked long and slow in oil give all three. The other dishes are green, acidic or cold, and beside any of them the same wine reads as pure tannin.
